title: Ignatius' cannonball
hook: a soldier's leg is shattered, and bored in bed he reads lives of saints

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Council of Trent and the Counter-Reformation, a church trying to fix itself. Your line was reform from within. What small broken thing did you fix from the inside? Day eight hundred seventy-three.

A fortress wall in Pamplona, in the north of Spain, under siege. The other defenders want to surrender. One young Basque nobleman talks them into fighting on. His name is Iñigo, and he loves fine clothes, swordplay and stories of knights. Then a cannonball comes over the wall and smashes his leg. The fortress falls. His enemies carry him home on a litter to his family's castle at Loyola. Surgeons set the leg badly, and it has to be broken and set again. A bone still juts out below the knee, and, by his own later account, he has it sawed off so the leg will look right in a close-fitting boot. Then there's nothing left to do but lie in bed. Today: Ignatius' cannonball.
screen: `NOTHING TO DO BUT LIE IN BED.`

segments.voice: Bored, he asks for something to read. He wants romances about knights and their ladies. The house doesn't have any. What it has is a life of Christ and a book of the lives of the saints. So he reads those, because there's nothing else. And here's what he noticed, later telling it about himself in the third person, calling himself the pilgrim. His mind kept switching between two daydreams. In one, he was a knight again, winning glory and the favor of a great lady. In the other, he was doing what Francis and Dominic did, walking barefoot, giving everything away. Both daydreams were pleasant while they lasted. But afterward, the knight daydream left him dry and restless, and the saint daydream left him quiet and content. He began to pay attention to that difference. Which thoughts leave you consoled? Which leave you empty? That small noticing in a sickbed became the root of what Jesuits call discernment, and of the Spiritual Exercises he would later write, a set of meditations people still make on retreats. When he could walk again, the soldier left his sword before an image of Mary, by his own account, and went off as a beggar and a pilgrim. Later, with friends, he founded the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits. Paul, in the King James Bible, hears God say: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." The cannonball didn't make Ignatius holy. It made him lie still long enough to notice. Wounded into holiness doesn't mean the wound was good. It means something good came through it.

Here's the practice: someone brave. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a brave person whose story you know. A saint, a grandparent, a nurse, someone from the news, someone from a book. Let their story play for a minute. Then do what Ignatius did in bed: notice what the story leaves behind in you. Restless, or quiet? Smaller, or steadier? Don't judge it. Just notice. If you pray, you can thank God for them. If you don't, just stay with them a while. Later today, read one page about them. The bell holds the time.
Ignatius' cannonball. The shot that smashed a soldier's leg and left him in bed with nothing to read but lives of Christ and the saints, where he learned to notice which thoughts left him content.

Your line: wounded into holiness. Today, when something stops you, a delay, a cold, a canceled plan, ask what you might notice in the stillness that you'd miss at full speed. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Ignatius of Loyola as a saint and as founder of the Jesuits; people of many churches make his Spiritual Exercises on retreats, and some end each day with a short review of which moments left them consoled or empty.

notes: Claims rule: no dates. Details from Ignatius' dictated Autobiography, ch. 1: defense of Pamplona when others wanted to surrender, cannonball wound, carried home by the French, the leg reset and a bone sawed for vanity (here: 'partly so it would look right in his boots'), no romances in the house, the life of Christ and lives of saints, the two daydreams and how they left him. Confirm each detail.
'calling himself the pilgrim' follows his third-person self-designation in the Autobiography; source paraphrased (quoted: null). Confirm.
Hanging his sword before the image of Our Lady at Montserrat given as 'tradition says' (it is also in the Autobiography); confirm.
howItsDone 'people of many churches' and the Examen: soften if needed.

Audit pass (serious): the Autobiography says the leg was rebroken because it was badly set, and the vanity motive was for sawing off a protruding bone; the hook had merged the two. Corrected. Sword at Montserrat is in the Autobiography itself, so now 'by his own account', not 'tradition says'.
